title: Chapter XXXV

teacherSummary.text: Darcy hands Elizabeth a letter explaining himself: he separated Bingley and Jane believing Jane indifferent and the Bennets improper; and Wickham squandered money, demanded more, and tried to elope with Darcy's 15-year-old sister Georgiana for her fortune.

vocabulary.context: But last summer he was again most painfully obtruded on my notice.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “obtrude”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I joined them unexpectedly a day or two before the intended elopement, and then Georgiana, unable to support the idea of grieving and offending a brother whom she almost looked up to as a father, acknowledged the whole to me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “elopement”: -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A frame consisting of two bars crossing each other at right angles and turning on a post or pin, to hinder the…
vocabulary.context: Darcy’s sometimes coming there stopped her, and instead of entering the park, she turned up the lane, which led her farther from the turnpike road.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “turnpike”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Wickham wrote to inform me that, having finally resolved against taking orders, he hoped I should not think it unreasonable for him to expect some more immediate pecuniary advantage, in lieu of the preferment, by which he could not be benefited.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “benefit”: be- (Old English be-, "thoroughly, about"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Departure, especially departure from this life
vocabulary.context: For about three years I heard little of him; but on the decease of the incumbent of the living which had been designed for him, he applied to me again by letter for the presentation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “decease”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Her look and manners were open, cheerful and engaging as ever, but without any symptom of peculiar regard, and I remained convinced from the evening’s scrutiny, that though she received his attentions with pleasure, she did not invite them by any participation of sentiment.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “symptom”: sym- (Greek syn, "together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To reverse or recant, as a previous decision
vocabulary.context: He spoke of it as a certain event, of which the time alone could be undecided.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “undecide”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of one who states anything
vocabulary.context: She was then but fifteen, which must be her excuse; and after stating her imprudence, I am happy to add, that I owed the knowledge of it to herself.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “stating”: stat (Latin stare, "to stand") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The condition of occupying the same place in space
vocabulary.context: His sisters’ uneasiness had been equally excited with my own; our coincidence of feeling was soon discovered; and, alike sensible that no time was to be lost in detaching their brother, we shortly resolved on joining him directly in London.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “coincidence”: -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Wickham wrote to inform me that, having finally resolved against taking orders, he hoped I should not think it unreasonable for him to expect some more immediate pecuniary advantage, in lieu of the preferment, by which he could not be benefited.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pecuniary”: -ary (Latin -arius, "connected with"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Letters in novels allow characters to speak fully; here the epistolary form reverses the plot.

significance: The letter shifts point of view, forcing Elizabeth (and readers) to re-examine the evidence.
discussionQuestions: How does the letter change what we know?
Where does point of view appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXV,” how does Austen show the letter? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXV develops the idea of the letter. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses point of view in Chapter XXXV to complicate the reader's understanding of the letter. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the letter responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the letter. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

options: The condition of occupying the same place in space
A frame consisting of two bars crossing each other at right angles and turning on a post or pin, to hinder the…

satQuestions.passage: Elizabeth awoke the next morning to the same thoughts and meditations which had at length closed her eyes. She could not yet recover from the surprise of what had happened; it was impossible to think of anything else, and totally indisposed for employment, she resolved soon after breakfast to indulge herself in air and exercise. She was proceeding directly to her favourite walk, when the recollection of Mr. Darcy’s sometimes coming there stopped her, and instead of entering the park, she turned up the lane, which led her farther from the turnpike road. The park paling was still the boundary on one side, and she soon passed one of the gates into the ground.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXXV”?

annotationFocus.lookFor: who is telling the story and what that narrator can and cannot know

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does the letter change what we know? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are obtruded, elopement, turnpike, benefited, decease. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “But last summer he was again most painfully obtruded on my notice.” Webster's says: To thrust impertinently. Now the word history: “obtrude”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “elopement”: -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “turnpike”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Letters in novels allow characters to speak fully; here the epistolary form reverses the plot. Why does this chapter matter? The letter shifts point of view, forcing Elizabeth (and readers) to re-examine the evidence. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see point of view, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the letter.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Point of view, Characterization, Plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Elizabeth awoke the next morning to the same thoughts and meditations which had at length closed her eyes. She could not yet recover from the surprise of what had happened; it was impossible to think of anything else, and totally indisposed for employment, she resolved soon after breakfast to indulge herself in air and exercise. She was proceeding directly to her favourite walk, when the recollection of Mr. Darcy’s sometimes coming there stopped her, and instead of entering the park, she turned up the lane, which led her farther from the turnpike road. The park paling was still the boundary on one side, and she soon passed one of the gates into the ground.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Characterization, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXXV,” how does Austen show the letter? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the letter, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes the letter. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
